bridge: S06 separated identity from permission. Here you will inspect a fictional account flow without attempting real sign-ins.
teaching:
### Map every entry route

List sign-in, password reset, recovery, remembered devices and any federation provider. An attacker may choose the weakest route. A strong password check does not help if recovery can transfer the account with weaker evidence.

### Avoid revealing unnecessary account information

Enumeration means discovering which accounts exist. Different messages, timings or response codes can disclose that information. Choose a response policy that balances privacy with useful recovery guidance, and test more than the displayed sentence.

### Protect recovery credentials

A reset token should have suitable unpredictability, lifetime and use restrictions. Bind it to the intended account and operation. Check what happens when a password changes or a token is reused.

Rate limits and abuse monitoring help constrain repeated guesses and message floods. Do not lock out legitimate users casually or rely on one IP address as the only identity.

### Recheck session handling

After successful sign-in or a privilege change, manage session identifiers appropriately. On logout or account restriction, document which sessions stop working and how soon. A button saying “signed out” is not proof that a previously issued credential is unusable.
example:
Fictional reset state
Token R1: account A, purpose password-reset, expires at 12:00, unused
11:59 R1 + valid new password -> accept, mark used
11:59 R1 second submission     -> reject used
12:01 fresh unused R1 scenario -> reject expired
R1 used as login session      -> reject wrong purpose
explanation: The second row follows the first, while the expired row is a separate fresh-state scenario. Keeping those sequences explicit prevents impossible test expectations. Token validation and consumption should be atomic enough that concurrent attempts cannot both succeed.
exercise: Trace the four supplied cases. Add a token for account B submitted to reset A, and a request with no token. State what must be checked and what a generic public response should avoid disclosing.
solution: Bind account/purpose, check expiry and unused state, then consume deliberately. Foreign-account and absent tokens reject. Public messages should avoid unnecessary account-existence disclosure; internal logs can retain safe reason codes.
challenge: Draw reset-request, issued, consumed and expired states. Give one concurrent-use test and one verification that a reset token cannot be used as an ordinary session credential.
challenge_solution: Paper transitions: request → issued/unused after approved generation; issued/unused → consumed after valid account/purpose/time checks and atomic redemption; issued/unused → expired at the deadline. Consumed and expired tokens cannot return to unused; a new request issues a different token. Concurrent case: two redemptions of the same unused token reach the protected consume step; at most one succeeds and the other sees consumed. Purpose case: submit the reset token to the ordinary session validator and expect rejection even before considering object access. Document whether a real password reset revokes old sessions; do not assume it does.
